source: Fauconnier (1985/1994) Mental Spaces: Aspects of Meaning Construction in Natural Language
finding: Founding statement. Mental spaces are small partial structures built on the fly while we talk and think, prompted by language. Space builders (in 1990, if, Max believes, in the picture) open a new space. Elements in one space link to counterparts in others. The Access Principle lets a name or description in one space reach its counterpart in another.
numbers: No experiment. Theory built from linguistic data: opacity, presupposition projection, counterfactuals, tense, pictures.
limits: Not an empirical psychology study; no effect sizes. Reissue of the 1985 MIT Press book. Only chapter previews were reachable this session.
agent_relevance: Direct template for S2: each hypothesis, belief or counterfactual lives in its own space with explicit counterpart links, never mixed into the base text.

source: Dinsmore (1991) Partitioned Representations
finding: Independent AI parallel to mental spaces. Knowledge is split into partitions (belief, fiction, time, hypothesis) and reasoning runs inside a partition. The same inference rules apply in every partition; what changes is which partition holds the premises.
numbers: No empirical numbers.
limits: Known only from a secondary mention (a review of Fauconnier called the idea powerful). Not read.
agent_relevance: Supports an engineering design: one inference machinery, many scoped stores. Matches S2 scoped hypotheses.

source: Fauconnier & Turner (1998) Conceptual Integration Networks
finding: Extends mental spaces to four-space networks: two input spaces, a generic space and a blended space. Selective projection from the inputs, then composition, completion and elaboration, produce new structure. Governed by optimality principles and about 20 vital relations.
numbers: Cognitive Science 22(2), 133-187. No experiment.
limits: Conceptual and illustrative. Detail on blends belongs to the sibling blending documents (02, 03, 04). Only the bibliographic record was reached.
agent_relevance: Spaces are the base layer; blending is only needed at an impasse (an operator), not at S2.

source: Fauconnier (2005) Compression and Emergent Structure
finding: Fauconnier restates the theory: counterfactuals, metaphor, framing, analogy and grammar all come from integration networks over mental spaces. Emergent structure in the blend is simpler than the inputs, and meaning sits in the whole network, not in one space. Worked example: complex numbers as a blend of the real line and 2D space, with new elements, a new operation (multiplication through angles) and a statement that is false in the blend but true in an input.
numbers: About 20 vital relations (Cause-Effect, Analogy, Time, Space, Change, Identity, Part-Whole, Representation).
quote: Meaning is not in any one space but in the entire integration network
limits: Theoretical essay with examples, no tests. Written by the theory's founder.
agent_relevance: A claim true inside one scoped space may be false in another, so every claim must carry its space tag.

source: Coulson (2005) Sarcasm and the Space Structuring Model
finding: A mental space is described as a partition of working memory. Sarcasm is explained by two counterfactual spaces, Expected Reaction and Counterfactual Trigger, plus a blend. Meaning lies in none of the spaces. The main comprehension demand is keeping track of counterparts across spaces. It predicts that anything that makes the two spaces more salient (an explicit echo) makes irony easier to see.
numbers: No new experiment in this chapter; it reviews others. Example 'I love people who signal' means just what it says, which breaks the 'opposite of literal' rule.
limits: The prediction is stated but the chapter reports no direct reading-time test of it.
agent_relevance: Processing cost is cross-space bookkeeping. For an LLM, each extra space adds a counterpart mapping that must be written out.

source: Coulson & Pascuale (c. 2008) For the sake of argument: Mourning the unborn and reviving the dead through conceptual blending
finding: Corpus analysis of real persuasive text (abortion rhetoric, the 'snowflake kid'). Serious arguments are made by building unrealistic blends from separate spaces (Past, Present, Blended). The Access Principle alone is not enough: a snowflake kid is frozen and tiny, which neither input says. Blending is limited by frames, the task and the community, not only by formal principles.
numbers: Qualitative; attested examples only, no statistics.
quote: Besides constitutive and governing principles, conceptual integration operations are greatly constrained by overall knowledge of the communicative event
limits: No behavioural data. Critics call the blending principles vague; the authors answer with discourse-level constraints. Publication year approximate.
agent_relevance: Spaces let a writer move a framing (murder) from one space to another. The agent must block frames crossing spaces without a stated link.

source: Veale, O'Donoghue & Keane (2000) Computation and Blending
finding: First tractable computational account of the many-space model. Sapper uses spreading activation over a semantic network and forms bridges between spaces. Argues a computational model keeps the theory from being a just-so story, and lets linguists run what-if tests on spaces.
numbers: No benchmark numbers; algorithmic model with worked cases.
limits: Dated (2000); small hand-built networks; no human data.
agent_relevance: A symbolic design for cross-space counterparts: link only what bridges connect, instead of pulling all knowledge into one context.

source: Brone (c. 2008) Hyper- and misunderstanding in interactional humor
finding: Applies mental spaces to conversational humour. Hyper-understanding exploits a weak spot in a prior utterance by echoing it while reversing its meaning. Misunderstanding is a real misreading by a character. Both are explained with layered viewpoint mental spaces (Clark's layers) and referential opacity.
numbers: Qualitative conversational data; no counts recorded.
limits: Corpus anecdotes; year approximate.
agent_relevance: Shows spaces tracking whose viewpoint holds a statement, as the agent needs to tag who said or believed each claim.

source: Coulson & Van Petten (2002) Conceptual integration and metaphor: an ERP study
finding: Event-related potential test of blending. Sentences with literal, mapping and metaphoric endings were compared. Metaphor and mapping gave a larger N400 than literal, read as extra mapping work, and the pattern was graded.
numbers: Memory and Cognition 30, 958-968. Amplitudes not recorded by me.
limits: Not opened. Numbers deliberately not stated. A graded N400 also fits other accounts (relevance, salience).
agent_relevance: Weak human evidence that space mapping costs processing. Do not lean on it.

source: Coulson (2001) Semantic Leaps: Frame-Shifting and Conceptual Blending in Meaning Construction
finding: Reports reading-time and ERP work on jokes and frame shifting; argues that frame-shifting needs cross-space mapping and costs time.
numbers: Exact timings not recorded by me.
limits: Not opened. Statements are from memory of the book and may be incomplete.
agent_relevance: Re-framing has a real cost, which supports G1: reframe only on a signal.

source: Steele, Wen & Han (2026) One mechanism for many mental spaces: a shared router over a value slot in language models
finding: The most direct test of Fauconnier in an LLM. Qwen, Pythia and Falcon3 (3B or smaller) keep a value in each non-actual space (painting, belief, dream, past, hypothetical). A low-rank space index subspace tags which space a value belongs to. A subspace trained on one space type controls the others. Belief is not specially separated from counterfactual, which fits Fauconnier's single Access Principle over the formal-semantics view.
numbers: Both values decodable: base 0.96 [0.95,0.97], alternative 0.94 [0.94,0.95] (n=240 per seed, chance 0.25). Alt-space colour 0.89-0.95 over 9 builder types. Cross-type transfer index 0.73 Qwen, 0.885 Pythia, 0.711 Falcon3 (bar 0.7 fixed in advance). Within-class transfer 0.89-0.92 vs between-class 0.53-0.76.
quote: A subspace trained to control one space type also controls the others
limits: Preprint; controlled templates; mechanistic results only on models of 3B or fewer. Companion paper not read. Falcon3 is weakest. Fictional (painting) source is a partial outlier.
agent_relevance: LLMs already hold scoped values inside the network. The scaffold should still write space tags in text, since the internal index is not under our control.

source: Steele et al. (2026), same paper: rank and hand-built steering
finding: Hand-built steering fails; learned subspaces work. Diff-of-means rank-1 equals a random direction. Effective rank of space directions is 4-5 of 10.
numbers: Random rank-1 flip 0.583; hand-built 0.583; DAS rank-1 0.883; rank-2 0.967; rank 4/8/16 1.000. Random 20-draw band [0.16,0.58].
limits: Leakage floor 0.58, so causal margins are over that floor, not over zero.
agent_relevance: Do not assume simple steering vectors give scope control; use explicit text structure.

source: Steele et al. (2026), same paper: report versus reasoning dissociation
finding: The value a model reports and the value it uses in a rule are controlled by different subspaces. Flipping the reported colour left the rule result unchanged, and the reverse.
numbers: Qwen2.5-3B: colour-trained subspace flips report 1.00, consequent 0.00; consequent-trained flips consequent 1.00, report 0.32. Falcon3: 1.00/0.49 and 0.29/1.00. Principal cosine 0.11 Qwen, 0.17 Falcon3. Pythia could not apply the rule.
limits: One rule (colour sorting); single seed per flip cell.
agent_relevance: Matches G2: written reasoning need not reflect what drove the answer, so check outputs by code.

source: Steele et al. (2026), same paper: building and nesting spaces
finding: Capable models read nested spaces at ceiling (past plus belief, reported speech, negation, belief nesting, counterfactual conditionals) with no bleed between frames. One exception: modal possibility ('might believe the cup is blue') collapses onto the actual value.
numbers: Compound and base both near 1.00, bleed near 0. Modal compound 0.04-0.62, with 0.4-0.96 of mass on the actual colour. At frontier scale (gpt-4o, Qwen2.5-72B, Gemini-2.5) models held eight coexisting spaces with no swap errors.
limits: Frontier results are behavioural and briefly reported; smaller models are weaker on past-belief in bare completion.
agent_relevance: Boundary: hypotheticals phrased as 'might' are the weak spot. Use explicit 'suppose X' scoped blocks, not modal hedges.

source: Li, Nye & Andreas (2021) Implicit representations of meaning in neural language models
finding: BART and T5 encode entities and their changing states in linearly readable form, like dynamic semantics. Editing those representations changes generated text. Exact state recovery is far from complete.
numbers: T5 probe recovers 14.3% of full information states in Alchemy and 53.8% in TextWorld. No-LM baseline 0% / 1.8%; no-change baseline 0% / 9.7%.
limits: Small synthetic worlds; probe and representation errors are not separable (authors say so). Kim and Schuster later criticised the Alchemy data.
agent_relevance: Early proof that discourse state is stored inside the model as a partial situation model.

source: Kim & Schuster (2023) Entity Tracking in Language Models
finding: Only code-trained GPT-3.5 tracks box contents through move operations; text-only GPT-3 and Flan-T5 do not. Alchemy success was mostly trivial cases.
numbers: In Alchemy 62.7% of probed beaker states equalled the initial state; with empty beakers 87.6% were trivial and only 12.4% tested change. Probe accuracy 86.8% on trivial, 3.1% on non-trivial. Finetuned T5 near-perfect on the base split, falling with more operations.
limits: Behavioural only; unclear why code pretraining helps. Toy cloze task.
agent_relevance: Scoped-state tracking is not automatic. Keep state in an explicit structure the program updates.

source: Wilf, Lee, Liang & Morency (2023) Think Twice: Perspective-Taking Improves LLM Theory-of-Mind
finding: SimToM: first filter the story to what character A knows (their space), then answer. This is like opening a belief space before querying it. Gains are large for weaker models.
numbers: BigTOM false belief: +29.5 pts over 0-shot and +14.2 over 0-shot CoT for GPT-3.5-Turbo. ToMI false belief: +16, +19, +47 pts over 0-shot CoT for Llama2-7b, Llama2-13b, GPT-3.5-Turbo. SC-CoT 33.5% vs SimToM 81.0% on FB. Oracle human perspectives lift ToMI FB 81.0 to 96 and BigTOM FB 70.5 to 96.0.
limits: Slight drop for GPT-4 on BigTOM (benchmark made with GPT-4). A two-step CoT control fell to 58.25% on BigTOM total, so the structure matters.
agent_relevance: Best direct support for S2: build the scoped view first, answer inside it. Gap to the oracle shows the filter step is the weak link.

source: Sclar et al. (2023) Minding Language Models' (Lack of) Theory of Mind: SymbolicToM
finding: A plug-in decoding algorithm keeps explicit graphs of what each character believes, including nested beliefs. This is a symbolic version of mental spaces. It is more robust than supervised models on harder variants.
numbers: GPT-3-Davinci on ToMi rises 38 absolute points, to 92% averaged over question types.
limits: Only abstract and introduction read closely; ToMi has template ambiguities.
agent_relevance: A tested design where code, not the model, holds the per-agent spaces. Fits the rule that the program holds state.

source: Zhu, Zhang & Wang (2024) Language Models Represent Beliefs of Self and Others
finding: Linear probes decode who believes what (self and other, true or false) from attention-head activations. Steering along these directions changes theory-of-mind scores.
numbers: A group of mid-layer heads gives over 80% validation accuracy for belief status (chance 50% binary, 25% four-way). Random perturbation has marginal effect. Steering toward the true-protagonist direction raises false-belief accuracy and slightly lowers true-belief accuracy.
limits: Mistral-7B and DeepSeek-7B; exact intervention gains are in figures and not copied here.
agent_relevance: Per-agent belief spaces are linearly present inside LLMs, adding to Steele et al.

source: Ullman (2023) Large Language Models Fail on Trivial Alterations to Theory-of-Mind Tasks
finding: Small changes that keep the ToM logic (for example a transparent container) turn earlier apparent success upside down. A critique of Kosinski's claim.
numbers: Probability tables on bag-content prompts; condition-by-condition numbers not recorded.
limits: A short note with a few hand-made prompts, no sample statistics. The author corrected an earlier claim after a double-space prompt error.
agent_relevance: Space tracking is brittle to surface changes. Test the scaffold on perturbed items.

source: Kim et al. (2023) FANTOM: stress-testing machine theory of mind in interactions
finding: In multi-party chats where people join and leave, models can pick the right belief answer yet fail the prerequisite questions (who could answer, who had access). This is illusory theory of mind. All models are far below humans.
numbers: Human All-score 87.5 on the main set (90.6 and 90.6 on the two list sets). GPT-4 0613 + CoT (June): 26.6 / 40.2 / 57.7; GPT-4 (Oct) + CoT: 14.8 / 31.4 / 41.1; Llama-2 Chat + CoT 0.4 / 6.0 / 7.8.
limits: Column labels partly rebuilt from garbled table text. Humans: 11 graduate students, 32 question sets.
agent_relevance: Belief answers without information-access bookkeeping are untrustworthy. Require the agent to list who knows what.

source: Li, Yu & Ettinger (2023) Counterfactual reasoning: testing language models' understanding of hypothetical scenarios
finding: Models partly switch to a counterfactual space ('if cats were vegetarians') but even in the counterfactual condition the preference for the counterfactual-congruent word is at best slightly above chance for most models. Only GPT-3 clearly prefers it. Models may rely on lexical triggers more than on counterfactual structure.
numbers: Small-scale Exp1, counterfactual-condition preference for the counterfactual-congruent word: BERT 53.1%, RoBERTa 68.8%, MPNet 46.9% (real-world condition BERT 34.4, RoBERTa 18.8). GPT rows not cleanly readable.
limits: Small models plus text-davinci-003; table parsed from layout text, so values are approximate.
agent_relevance: Weak space switching in small models. Mark a hypothetical explicitly; do not rely on inference.

source: Wu et al. (2023) Reasoning or Reciting? Exploring the Capabilities and Limitations of LMs Through Counterfactual Tasks
finding: Models do well on default tasks but drop consistently on counterfactual variants of 11 tasks (base-9 arithmetic, altered chess, altered code semantics) even when the altered world is stated in the prompt. Suggests partial overfitting to default conditions.
numbers: 11 tasks; GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Claude, PaLM-2; counterfactual accuracy above chance but substantially below default on each task. In spatial reasoning GPT-4 is best on default and has the largest counterfactual drop.
limits: Per-task numbers not copied. Authors accept part of the gap is an expected train-test gap.
agent_relevance: A stated hypothetical space leaks default-world habits. After S2 builds a space, S4 must test it against held-out checks (G3).

source: Shi et al. (2023) Large Language Models Can Be Easily Distracted by Irrelevant Context
finding: One irrelevant sentence in a grade-school maths problem sharply cuts accuracy. Fewer than 30% of base problems are solved consistently across distractor variants. Least-to-most prompting is the most robust; exemplars with distractors help.
numbers: GSM-IC on code-davinci-002 and text-davinci-003: significant drop for all prompting methods; macro accuracy under 30%.
limits: GPT-3 era models. The distractor is irrelevant text, not a rival hypothesis.
agent_relevance: Out-of-scope material in the working context hurts. Supports separate spaces and the S1 input hygiene step.

source: Weston & Sukhbaatar (2023) System 2 Attention
finding: Regenerating the context to keep only the relevant parts, then answering from the clean context, beats using the raw context. Keeping the original beside it lowers the gain.
numbers: Factual QA with a distractor opinion: LLaMA-2-70B-chat 62.8% to 80.3% with S2A (instruction-only debias prompt 71.7%). GSM-IC in-topic distractors 51.7% to 61.3%. Objectivity on long arguments +57.4%.
limits: Costs an extra generation call; LLaMA-2 era.
agent_relevance: A clean scoped context beats a mixed one; leaving the original in view erodes the gain.

source: Andreas (2022) Language Models as Agent Models
finding: Argues that LMs infer a model of the agent that produced the text, so they can act as if they hold beliefs and goals scoped to that agent.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Downloaded but not read before the shared scratch folder was cleared by another process. Position paper.
agent_relevance: Frames why per-agent or per-hypothesis scoping can work inside an LLM at all.
